newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs vote for Senate amid widespread apathy.
newsitem.headline: Czechs vote for Senate amid widespread apathy.

text.p: Czechs complete voting in the first round of Senate elections on Saturday amid signs of widespread voter apathy which could cloud the future of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's minority government.

The Czech news agency CTK quoted election officials as saying turnout on Friday, the first day of the two-day round, had averaged only about 20 percent despite an appeal from President Vaclav Havel for Czechs to vote in large numbers.

Pundits have billed the Senate elections as an indicator of whether the Czech Republic can break out of a political impasse following inconclusive lower house polls which stripped Klaus's conservative coalition of its majority last June.

But analysts said that if turnout fell well below 50 percent the real winners would not be Klaus or the opposition Social Democrat leader Milos Zeman, but the far-Right Republicans who are boycotting the Senate altogether.
Pre-election opinion polls suggested that turnout would be a little over half the electorate and one survey said 53 percent of respondents questioned the very need for a Senate.
Most opinion polls showed support for Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) roughly level with the Social Democrats on about 26 percent each, although one late poll showed ODS pulling ahead.
Analysts said a late surge in voting before the polls close at 2 pm (1300 GMT) was still possible.

But the signs were not good. "I don't know the candidates here, so I don't have to go and vote. Most of my friends don't like the Senate so they won't vote either," said Filip Eisenreich, a 20-year-old accounting assistant in Prague.
Conventional wisdom has been that if Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) did well in the Senate, he might provoke early lower house polls to regain the coalition's majority.
If ODS lost to the Social Democrats, however, Klaus could be forced to resign after seven years leading Czech economic reform first as finance minister and since 1992 as premier.
But Jiri Pehe, research director at the Open Media Research Institute (OMRI), said these theories may not be valid.

ODS is generally better at mobilising its supporters than the Social Democrats when public interest is low. A big ODS win on a low turnout might therefore not be representative for lower house polls, where 76.4 percent voted last June.
"If there is a low turnout, even if Klaus wins, I think that it would be very difficult for the ODS to know the real mood of the country," he said.
Many ordinary Czechs complain that they do not know what the Senate will do, and the country's government and opposition leaders all sit in the lower Chamber of Deputies.
The voting rules are also unfamiliar. The Senate will be elected under a British-style first past the post system unlike the proportional representation used in the lower house.
A run-off will be held on November 22-23 for the top two candidates in the first round if nobody wins more than half the vote. Run-offs are likely in most if not all 81 constituencies.
Pehe said Czech politics would be the loser if apathy was extreme. "If turnout is only 30 percent it would be a victory not for Klaus or Zeman but for the Republicans," he said.

The Republicans won eight percent in June on a platform against the political establishment and the gypsy minority, who are subjected to widespread discrimination. But they are boycotting the Senate as a waste of time and money.

The Senate has had a difficult birth. It was written into the new constitution of the Czech Republic which came into force in 1993 after the breakup of Czechoslovakia. But only now, almost four years later, is the Senate to be elected after much political footdragging.
